paper_title: EDGAR: Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement via Synthetic Failure

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient and photorealistic head avatar reconstruction, yet monocular video-based or image-based methods still suffer from under-constrained geometry and texture, leading to artifacts such as blurring, stretching, and temporal instability. We present EDGAR (Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement), a conditional diffusion framework designed to enhance the quality of Gaussian avatars by correcting artifacts while preserving identity fidelity. To train EDGAR, we construct EDGAR-SET, a hybrid triplet dataset composed of real-captured and synthetic-rendered samples, which simulates realistic Gaussian avatar failure cases by pairing degraded renderings with ground-truth and reference images. EDGAR refines degraded frames through a fusion block that injects identity features extracted by the self-supervised Sapiens model into a one-step diffusion backbone, enabling effective artifact removal without sacrificing efficiency. Our EDGAR model incorporates a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to address diverse degradation types and severity levels. The refined multi-view renderings are subsequently used as pseudo-targets to optimize a single underlying Gaussian avatar, so that the final avatar can be rendered without applying EDGAR to every output frame. Experiments on three different Gaussian avatar reconstruction methods, each evaluated under three different settings, show improvements in both perceptual and reconstruction measures over the raw outputs and an SDEdit-style refinement baseline. In addition, cross-view evaluation demonstrates improved calibrated consistency, while tests under large yaw and open-mouth expressions verify robustness under extreme settings. These results collectively indicate a useful operating regime for recoverable appearance artifacts. The code is available at https://kwanyun.github.io/edgar/

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Personalized head avatars are now integral to social gaming, VR telepresence, and mixed-reality interfaces, where users demand both photorealism and low latency. Mesh-based reconstruction pipelines [Feng et al. 2021; Lattas et al. 2020] offer the advantage of compact representations and practical usability thanks to their fixed mesh structure. However, reliance on meshes makes it difficult to capture high-frequency details and to scale to high-resolution geometry, particularly in regions such as hair. In contrast, recent 2 Yun et al. efforts built on volumetric neural-radiance fields (NeRF) [Mildenhall et al. 2021] have achieved impressive view synthesis results. Unfortunately, these methods require heavy per-scene optimization and remain slow for interactive use [Kirschstein et al. 2023; Zheng et al. 2022a; Zielonka et al. 2023]. Similarly, GAN-driven work achieved striking 3D-aware imagery [An et al. 2023; Li et al. 2023; Ye et al. 2023], yet encoded geometry only implicitly, limiting direct control over facial animation. These achievements have established the visual-quality bar while exposing the need for representations that are simultaneously lightweight, editable, and real-time ready. The field has since pivoted to rasterizable 3D Gaussian splats [Kerbl et al. 2023], which replace dense ray-marching with set of anisotropic blobs that are both GPU-friendly and easily deformed. Multi-view pipelines [Giebenhain et al. 2024; Hu et al. 2024; Xu et al. 2024] reach fast render times while faithfully tracking the face and producing realistically synthesized expressions. Monocularvideo [Chen et al. 2025, 2024; Qian et al. 2024b; Zhang et al. 2025] methods lower the capture barrier for further usability. Together, these Gaussian-based methods retain the photorealism pioneered by NeRF systems while unlocking interactive performance and casual acquisition, bringing personalized avatars within reach of everyday applications. Nevertheless, compressing capture into monocular video still leaves the reconstruction problem severely under-constrained. Monocular pipelines must infer geometry and texture in unobserved regions, which often causes artifactssuch as texture stretching, floating hair, or depth ambiguitieswhen rendering side profiles, wide-open mouths, or raised eyebrows. These issues are largely absent in avatars reconstructed from dense camera arrays, whereas limited observations in monocular settings leave unobserved regions under-constrained. While few recent methods utilize diffusionbased image generation to fill this gap by adding and removing noise using pretrained generative models [Meng et al. 2021] to refine the output [Wu et al. 2025a, 2024a], these approaches inherently involve guessing appearance from limited prior, thus failing to reliably preserve identity details, especially in unseen poses and expressions. To close this quality gap, we address avatar enhancement through diffusion-prior-based refinement framework, which we term Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement (EDGAR). Diffusion-based refinement is particularly well suited to this problem because strong generative priors can recover plausible highfrequency details while preserving overall visual realism under rendering degradation. The core idea is straightforward: given rendered frame from noisy or blurry Gaussian avatar and reference image of the subject, EDGAR learns to refine the output into sharper and more faithful rendering. This enables us to take an arbitrary Gaussian avatareven when trained under suboptimal monocular conditionsand upgrade it to higher visual quality. However, learning this mapping is non-trivial: there is no existing dataset of "imperfect avatar vs. ground-truth render" pairs, and the appearance of degraded avatar is not uniquely defined. To address this, we construct EDGAR-SET, hybrid dataset that combines real human data with synthetically generated samples to increase diversity in both identity and viewpoints. The dataset is organized as triplets: (1) rendered images from degraded avatars, (2) corresponding ground-truth images, and (3) reference identity images, as shown on the left of Figure 1. The synthetic component enables controlled simulation of realistic failure modes (e.g., sparseview training, unseen poses, and expression variations), while the human dataset grounds the model in real-world appearance distributions. This combination ensures broad coverage over identity, pose, and rendering artifacts. EDGAR learns conditional refinement function by injecting reference features [Khirodkar et al. 2024] into single-step diffusion backbone [Sauer et al. 2024]. To robustly handle diverse failure modes, we further adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, allowing the model to specialize across different types and severities of degradation. In addition, we use an expression consistency loss to encourage preservation of facial dynamics and subtle muscle movements during refinement. Our results demonstrate that EDGAR improves overall rendering fidelity and perceptual quality. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We construct EDGAR-SET, hybrid collection of paired Gaussian-avatar failures, ground-truth targets, and identity references designed around recoverable head-avatar artifacts. We introduce EDGAR, an efficient diffusion-driven refinement framework that learns to correct rendered artifacts of animatable Gaussian head avatars and distills the refined 2D targets back into the underlying 3D avatar. We develop subject-reference conditioning and expressionaware supervision to preserve identity and facial motion during refinement, together with lightweight MoE module that handles diverse degradation patterns without increasing the final avatar rendering cost.

2 Related Work
2.1 Head Reconstruction
sections.content: Classical head reconstruction leverages priors from 3D morphable models (3DMMs) [Blanz and Vetter 1999; Cao et al. 2013; Li et al. 2017] to recover identity and expression from images or videos. Unlike video based retargeting [Guo et al. 2024; Zhao et al. 2025], 3D reconstruction provides explicit geometric and appearance representations, enabling more controllable and physically grounded avatar generation. Building on 3DMM priors, many methods tackle monocular reconstruction and tracking with varying levels of geometric detail and expression, either through classical fitting [Blanz and Vetter 2003; Cao et al. 2014; Romdhani and Vetter 2005; Thies et al. 2016] or, more recently, learning-based methods [Daněček et al. 2022; Deng et al. 2019; Zhu et al. 2016]. While these methods are efficient and provide explicit control through constructed blendshape parameters, their expressiveness in both dynamic geometry and subtle details is limited due to the constraints of the constructed space of defined 3DMM. To enhance quality beyond the linear expressiveness of 3DMMs, recent approaches adopt implicit neural representations such as SDF [Park et al. 2019], OccupancyNet [Mescheder et al. 2019], NeRF [Mildenhall et al. 2021], and Instant-NGP [Müller et al. 2022]. Thanks EDGAR : Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement via Synthetic Failure 3 to their flexibility, these representations enable effective reconstruction of fine geometric details such as hair wisps and beards [Giebenhain et al. 2023; Zheng et al. 2022b,a, 2023; Zielonka et al. 2023]. These advances have substantially improved the realism of head avatars, but often at the cost of high computational complexity or slow rendering speed, which limits their practicality in interactive applications.

sections.title: 2.2 Gaussian Head Avatars
sections.content: Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. 2023] has emerged as an efficient representation for photorealistic scene rendering. Instead of representing geometry with an explicit mesh or an implicit neural field, 3DGS models scene as collection of learnable 3D Gaussians, each associated with attributes such as position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color. These Gaussians are rasterized efficiently, enabling high-quality rendering at interactive frame rates. When adapted to dynamic human faces, this representation gives rise to Gaussian head avatars, which model facial appearance and deformation using set of animatable Gaussians. Compared with prior implicit representations, Gaussian head avatars offer favorable balance between visual fidelity, rendering efficiency, and editability. Based on the number of input views, Gaussian avatar reconstruction methods can be broadly divided into two categories. Multiview methods based on calibrated camera arrays [Aneja et al. 2025; Giebenhain et al. 2024; Qian et al. 2024a; Sun et al. 2025; Teotia et al. 2024; Xu et al. 2024] achieve highly photorealistic reconstructions across diverse viewpoints and expressions, benefiting from dense observations of each subject. However, collecting such data requires specialized multi-camera capture systems, which greatly limits scalability and accessibility. To reduce this burden, recent works have explored monocular video-based methods [Chen et al. 2024; Ma et al. 2024; Moon et al. 2025; Shao et al. 2024; Song et al. 2025; Teotia et al. 2025; Wei et al. 2025a,b; Xiang et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2025] and few-image-based methods [Chu and Harada 2024; He et al. 2025; Kirschstein et al. 2025; Taubner et al. 2025b,a; Zheng et al. 2025]. These methods incorporate additional priors, such as FLAME fitting [Li et al. 2017] or semantic feature extraction [Oquab et al. 2023], to compensate for the lack of observations during training. Nevertheless, Gaussian head avatars reconstructed from limited inputs remain fundamentally under-constrained. As result, they often exhibit artifacts such as blurry textures, floating Gaussians, and unstable geometry in regions that are weakly observed during training. In contrast, multi-view Gaussian avatars typically provide cleaner and more stable renderings because their geometry and appearance are better constrained by dense observations. Our work is motivated by this gap: we aim to learn how degraded Gaussian avatar renderings should be refined using supervision derived from high-quality data, and to apply this knowledge to improve avatars reconstructed under sparse-view or monocular conditions. et al. 2021] and editing [Lugmayr et al. 2022; Meng et al. 2021; Rombach et al. 2022]. This capability stems from expressive latent priors learned from large-scale data, which capture rich distributions of natural images. Such priors enable models both to generate photorealistic samples and to guide the refinement of degraded or incomplete inputs toward plausible, high-quality outputs. While most refinement methods have been developed for super-resolution [Wang et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2024b] and restoration [Luo et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2025b; Zhang et al. 2024] in general scenes or images, only few methods have been applied to human faces or avatars. GAN-based methods typically encode images into the latent space of pretrained model and then pass them through the generator again to produce modified images in 2D [Abdal et al. 2019; Richardson et al. 2021a,b; Yun et al. 2024] or 3D [Jiang et al. 2022; Sun et al. 2022; Yun et al. 2025]. These methods require images to be cropped and aligned. More closely related to our work, recent works [Lee et al. 2025; Wu et al. 2025a, 2024a] utilize an SDEdit-like [Meng et al. 2021] approach that adds noise and removes it to refine rendered avatars. While SDEdit-style refinement is effective for blind restoration, the network lacks explicit knowledge of how the avatar should look, and the stochastic noise-adding procedure introduces randomness. Consequently, the denoising step may produce inconsistent results across frames, leading to temporal jittering. Difix3D+ [Wu et al. 2025b] more directly couples single-step diffusion refiner with optimization of static NeRF and 3DGS representations. EDGAR applies related refinement strategy to animatable Gaussian head avatars, using paired avatar failures, subject reference, and expression supervision to preserve identity and facial motion. Larger image-editing foundation models may offer higher single-frame quality, but avatar refinement also requires identity, expression, and cross-view consistency. EDGAR addresses these requirements through avatar-specific supervision and shared 3D optimization, without per-frame diffusion inference.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Our goal is to design model that refines rendered Gaussian avatars trained under diverse conditions, where limited observations often lead to visual artifacts. Specifically, we formulate avatar enhancement as diffusion-prior-based refinement task: given degraded rendering and subject reference image, the model learns to produce sharper and more faithful output. To enable this, we construct EDGAR-SET (Section 3.1), triplet dataset that simulates realistic failure modes and provides paired ground-truth supervision. Building on this dataset, we train EDGAR, diffusion-based refinement network conditioned on reference identity features, to correct artifacts while preserving subject fidelity (Section 3.2). Finally, we optimize the underlying Gaussian avatar itself using EDGAR-refined renderings as supervision, allowing the improvements to be absorbed into the 3D representation while preserving the efficiency of the original avatar model (Section 3.4).

The reference image 𝐼𝑟 is drawn from ground-truth rendering of the same subject under different view and/or expression, supplying appearance cues that guide refinement. At inference time, 𝐼𝑟 corresponds to frame from the monocular video used to train the avatar. Given degraded input 𝐼𝑓 and its reference 𝐼𝑟 , EDGAR learns to generate refined output ˆ𝐼𝑓 that faithfully approximates the ground truth 𝐼𝑔𝑡 . To construct EDGAR-SET, we define three key requirements to ensure effective training for avatar refinement. First, the dataset must contain diverse identities to support generalization across subjects. Second, it should include challenging conditions such as novel viewpoints, which are primary sources of artifacts in Gaussian avatar rendering. Third, each triplet must include reference image that differs from the ground-truth target while still providing meaningful identity and appearance cues under varying poses or expressions. To satisfy these criteria, we design EDGAR-SET as hybrid dataset that combines real-captured data with large-scale synthetic augmentation, enabling both realism and broad coverage of edge cases. Following these guidelines, we construct EDGAR-SET using both real and synthetic data sources. For real data, we leverage the calibrated multi-view corpus NeRSemble [Kirschstein et al. 2023] and build avatars using the RGBAvatar pipeline [Li et al. 2025], which provides high-fidelity reconstructions grounded in real-world appearance. For synthetic data, we incorporate the CAFCA [Buehler et al. 2024] corpus, which significantly expands identity diversity and introduces extreme view directions and expressions that are difficult to capture in real-world settings. Using CAFCA, we construct avatars based on the original 3D Gaussian Splatting formulation [Kerbl et al. 2023], enabling the systematic simulation of wide range of degradation patterns. The degradation patterns include floating Gaussian artifacts, blurry or over-smoothed regions, misaligned geometry, and view-dependent inconsistencies. The synthetic split primarily exhibits moderate failures due to larger number of input views, while the real-captured split introduces more extreme failure modes, such as severe geometric distortions caused by limited-view reconstruction. Across both datasets, we vary training EDGAR : Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement via Synthetic Failure 5 conditionssuch as the number of input viewsto induce realistic failure cases. After constructing avatars, we obtain degraded renderings 𝐼𝑓 alongside their corresponding ground-truth images 𝐼𝑔𝑡 , and sample distinct ground-truth frame as the reference 𝐼𝑟 . This unified pipeline yields diverse triplets that cover both realistic and extreme scenarios, enabling EDGAR to learn robust refinement across broad spectrum of avatar artifacts. In this way, our triplet formulation extends the utility of the original datasets beyond static ground-truth collections. Specifically, our triplet formulation converts the original datasets into supervised training data for refinement by simulating failures under diverse scenarios and incorporating reference images. In contrast, the original datasets (NeRSemble and CAFCA) primarily provide ground-truth observations without explicit degradation modeling. From this raw triplet set, we filter out images with severe artifacts where 𝐼𝑓 diverges significantly from 𝐼𝑔𝑡 , making them unsuitable for training. We compute LPIPS scores as similarity measure and discard cases with consistently low similarity. As shown in Figure 2, triplets in which expression fidelity is lost or artifacts are irreparable are removed, while cases with degraded but recoverable qualitysuch as Gaussian noise artifacts with consistent expression and head poseare retained. After this filtering step, the final EDGAR-SET, consisting of 400K high-resolution images across thousands of identities, is constructed. Configuration of EDGAR-SET is summarized in Figure 3. EDGAR-SET adheres to the guidelines established for training EDGAR, including diverse identities, expressions, and viewpoints, as well as the inclusion of reference images. The resulting training regime emphasizes recoverable appearance artifacts and moderate reconstruction errors, whereas severe structural failures are not represented reliably by the available image and reference pairs. The residual blocks are responsible for timestep injection, while the cross-attention layers handle prompt conditioningneither of which we aim to modify. sections.title: 3.4 Avatar Refinement
sections.content: After training EDGAR, we use it to further refine the underlying Gaussian avatar itself. Given Gaussian avatar as input, we first render it from multiple views and then apply EDGAR to each rendered image to obtain refined images ˆ𝐼𝑓 . These refined images are subsequently used as supervision signals to optimize the Gaussian avatar parameters with an ℓ1 loss and an SSIM loss. Unlike prior refinement EDGAR : Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement via Synthetic Failure 7 strategies that split or add Gaussians during optimization, we do not perform such operations, as they increase the number of Gaussians and lead to slower rendering. Our goal is to improve reconstruction quality while preserving the efficiency of the original model. During the refinement stage, single reference image 𝐼𝑟 is randomly selected and used throughout the process. This refinement process is shown in Figure 5. Importantly, EDGAR is not used only as post-processing module after rendering. Instead, its refined outputs are further used as optimization targets for the Gaussian avatar. In this way, the improvements introduced by EDGAR are absorbed into the 3D representation itself, allowing the refined avatar to produce higherquality renderings directly. Because the refinement is performed by optimizing single shared 3D Gaussian representation across multiview rendered images, the resulting updates remain consistent in 3D and improve cross-view coherence. sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content: We implemented and ran our data-construction pipeline using RGBAvatar and 3DGS on computer equipped with single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. For the real-capture split of EDGAR-SET, we used RGBAvatar with the NeRSemble [Kirschstein et al. 2023] dataset, varying the number of viewpoints, and performed selfreenactment to construct EDGAR-SET of 99 identities. Using 3DGS with CAFCA [Buehler et al. 2024], we also constructed synthetic split of EDGAR-SET of 1,500 identities with varying expressions, lighting conditions, and camera positions. While the real-capture split was constructed using 1 to 4 viewpoints during training, the synthetic split was constructed using only multi-view settings, specifically at least with 5 viewpoints, because 3DGS cannot reconstruct an avatar from single viewpoint. All images were resized to 512512 for both training and testing. sections.title: 4.2 Baseline Comparison
sections.content: EDGAR is general Gaussian avatar refinement framework and can be applied to arbitrary trained or optimized Gaussian avatar reconstruction methods. To evaluate its effectiveness, we conducted experiments on three different baselines: CAP4D [Taubner et al. 2025a], which is singleto multi-image-based reconstruction method, GaussianAvatars [Qian et al. 2024a], which enables high-quality avatar reconstruction from multi-view videos, and RGBAvatar [Li et al. 2025], which is single-video-based reconstruction method. These three methods represent complementary design choices, ranging from single-image-based and single-video-based to multi-view settings, providing comprehensive benchmark for assessing EDGARs refinement capability across different reconstruction settings. For comprehensive evaluation, because each method supports reconstruction from different number of inputs, we conducted comparisons using avatars reconstructed with varying numbers of inputs. Specifically, we used 1, 4, and 8 images for CAP4D, 1, 4, and 8 videos for RGBAvatar, and 8, 10, and 12 videos for GaussianAvatars, following the settings used in each method. Note that RGBAvatar was used during data construction and is included here as an auxiliary test baseline. For testing, we used ten unseen identities from NeRSemble for self-reenactment and additionally six different identities from the INSTA [Zielonka et al. 2023] dataset for cross-identity reenactment, and all comparisons were conducted on novel views. In addition, following prior studies [Lee et al. 2025; Wu et al. 2025a, 2024a], we also applied an SDEdit-style refinement baseline to the generated avatars. Specifically, SD-Turbo was utilized, which is equivalent to EDGARs backbone model with the timestep set to 𝜏 = 250 for noise injection and denoising. This enables direct comparison between our refinement approach and diffusion-based editing methods widely used in 3D character generation. Figure 6 presents EDGAR results for avatars reconstructed by CAP4D [Taubner et al. 2025a], GaussianAvatars [Qian et al. 2024a], and RGBAvatar [Li et al. 2025] under different input settings. Relative to the unrefined outputs, EDGAR reduces blurring and Gaussian artifacts while recovering fine facial details such as hair and skin texture. In contrast, the SDEdit-style refinement often introduced stochastic variations, leading to oversmooth texture and identity drift. These qualitative comparisons illustrate EDGARs refinement behavior across Gaussian avatars generated by different reconstruction methods. To further demonstrate performance on the same identity, Figure 8 complements Figure 6 by presenting the results of the three pipelines on the same identity and frame. 8 Yun et al. Fig. 6. sections.title: 4.3 Temporal Evaluation and Cost Analysis
sections.content: We measured foreground temporal warping error (tWE) on 100 consecutive frames for each NeRSemble test identity. Dense optical flow and bidirectional cycle-consistency validity mask were estimated from each unrefined Base sequence, where the same correspondences were used for Base and EDGAR. We computed the mean RGB 𝐿1 difference after warping on valid foreground pixels at 256 256 resolution and averaged the errors over the 99 transitions within each identity. We report the mean and standard deviation across identities. As presented in Table 7, EDGAR lowered tWE for CAP4D and RGBAvatar but raised it for GaussianAvatars, although the average tWE across pipelines decreased. This metric measures motion-compensated photometric stability, complementing the spatial-fidelity evaluations. For the cost analysis, we estimated Base-avatar optimization times for CAP4D, RGBAvatar, and GaussianAvatars and measured the complete EDGAR refinement time. Base reconstruction times were based on 100,000 CAP4D updates, 60,000 RGBAvatar updates, and 750,000 GaussianAvatars updates. They exclude preprocessing and CAP4Ds separate upstream multi-view synthesis stage, reported to require approximately four hours [Taubner et al. 2025a]. As presented in Table 8, complete EDGAR refinement required 5.04, 7.96, and 16.60 minutes on average, respectively. Importantly, EDGAR incurs only one-time refinement cost and adds no inference-time overhead: the refined avatars preserve the original Gaussian count and rendering path. In our experiments, output throughput remained within 2% of the base models and increased slightly in two of the three pipelines. sections.title: 4.7 User Study
sections.content: To further assess the perceptual quality of refined avatars, we conducted web-based user study with 15 participants, with an average age of 27.6 years, including 7 males and 8 females. Each participant was presented with 20 randomized pairs of avatar renderings shown as video sequences generated by the baseline methods (CAP4D and CAP4D+SDEdit) and our method, EDGAR. Each pair consisted of cross-reenactment results, along with the source identity as reference for identity comparison, and were displayed side-by-side in randomized order to avoid positional bias. Participants were asked to choose their preferred result with respect to three criteria: animation quality, identity preservation, and overall avatar preference. As shown in Table 11, EDGAR was consistently preferred over both baselines across all evaluation criteria. Compared with CAP4D, EDGAR achieved preference rates of 87.33% in animation quality, 91.33% in identity preservation, and 96.67% in overall avatar preference. The preference margin was even larger when compared with CAP4D+SDEdit, where EDGAR achieved 94.67%, 98.0%, and 98.0% for the three criteria, respectively. These outcomes align with our quantitative findings, indicating that EDGAR not only improves animation quality and identity preservation, but also yields avatars that are perceived by participants as more visually convincing overall.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced EDGAR, diffusion-driven refinement framework for Gaussian head avatars. EDGAR adapts single-step image refinement to animatable heads through paired avatar-failure data, subjectreference conditioning, expression-aware supervision, and an auxiliary MoE module. Experiments on CAP4D, RGBAvatar, and GaussianAvatars demonstrate improvements in perceptual and reconstruction quality, with gains depending on the starting avatar and evaluation metric. The shared-avatar update retains approximately the Base rendering rate and improves calibrated cross-view consistency for CAP4D and GaussianAvatars. The pose-and-expression evaluation shows benefits under large yaw and open-mouth conditions. Limitations and Future Work. EDGAR is trained on structurally recoverable degradations: EDGAR-SET filters sourcetarget pairs with large LPIPS differences. Consequently, severe structural errors and artifacts in unobserved regions can remain after refinement, as illustrated in Figure 6. Recovering such failures may require additional observations or geometric supervision. Independently refined pseudo-targets can disagree across views, causing the shared Gaussian representation to average conflicting details or retain view-dependent errors. Although our cross-view evaluation shows that EDGAR generally improves 3D consistency, explicit multi-view constraints and confidence-aware selection of refined targets could further reduce such inconsistencies. Mouth interiors and translucent appearance also remain challenging. In addition, the temporal evaluation shows that the mean tWE decreased for CAP4D and RGBAvatar but increased for GaussianAvatars, indicating that improvements in spatial fidelity do not necessarily translate into greater temporal stability across all reconstruction pipelines. Explicit temporal supervision and improved modeling of dynamic facial regions are promising directions for future work. 14 Yun et al.
